'''''Houttuynia cordata''''', also known as '''fish mint''', '''fish leaf''', '''rainbow plant''', '''chameleon plant''', '''heart leaf''', '''fish wort''', or '''Chinese lizard tail''', is one of two species in the genus ''[[Houttuynia]]'' (the other being ''H. emeiensis''). It is a [[flowering plant]] native to [[Southeast Asia]].<ref name="rhs">{{cite web|title=''Houttuynia cordata'', Thunb.|url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:927252-1|publisher=KewScience, The Royal Horticultural Society, UK|access-date=8 October 2018|date=2018}}</ref> It grows in moist, shady locations.<ref name="pfaf">{{cite web |url=https://www.pfaf.org/user/plant.aspx?latinname=Houttuynia+cordata |title=''Houttuynia cordata'' Thunb.|publisher=Plants for a Future|date=2012|access-date=9 April 2018}}</ref> It was named after [[Martinus Houttuyn]].

==Growth==
''Houttuynia cordata'' is a [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]] that can grow to {{convert|0.6|-|1|m|ftin|abbr=on}}, spreading up to {{convert|1|m|ftin|abbr=on}}.<ref name=pfaf/><ref name=rhs/> The proximal part of the stem is trailing and produces [[adventitious root]]s, while the distal part of the stem grows vertically. The [[Leaf|leaves]] are alternate, broadly heart-shaped, {{convert|4-9|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|3-8|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} broad. Its [[flower]]s are greenish-yellow and borne on a terminal spike {{convert|2–3|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} long with four to six large white basal [[bract]]s.<ref name=pfaf/><ref name=rhs/> It normally blooms in the summer.

It is considered an invasive plant because of its ability to regrow rhizomes from any segment of its foliage.<ref>{{cite web |title=Houttuynia cordata (Chameleon Plant, Rainbow Plant) |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/houttuynia-cordata/|access-date=2020-09-29 |work=North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
It is native to Nepal, Taiwan, Myanmar, Bhutan, India, Indonesia, Japan, China, Thailand, Vietnam and Korea.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=생물종 상세정보 약모밀 |trans-title=Species details - ''Houttuynia cordata'' |url=https://species.nibr.go.kr/home/mainHome.do?contCd=009002&ktsn=120000060081 |access-date=2025-05-27 |work=National Institute of Biological Resources |language=ko}}</ref> In South Korea, it is found in [[North Gyeongsang Province|Gyeongsangbuk-do]], [[Ulleungdo]], and the Southern region.<ref name=":0" />

==Cultivation==
[[File:Houttuynia cordata Chameleon.jpg|thumb|right|''Houttuynia cordata'' 'Chameleon']]
''Houttuynia cordata'' grows in moist to wet soil or slightly submerged in water, as long as it is exposed partially or fully to the sun.<ref name=pfaf/><ref name=rhs/> It can become invasive in gardens and difficult to eradicate as its roots run deep and actively spread. It can be propagated by [[Division (horticulture)|division]].

It is usually found in one of its cultivated forms in temperate gardens. The 'Chameleon' variety (synonymous with ''H.cordata'' 'Court Jester', 'Tricolour', and 'Variegata') is slightly less vigorous than the parent species, with stubbier leaves mottled in both yellow and red. Another common variety, 'Flore Pleno', has masses of white bracts and retains the vigor of the parent species.

''Houttuynia cordata'' has been naturalized in North America.<ref>[http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=854 Global Invasive Species Database: Houttuynia cordata] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090206171023/http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=854 |date=6 February 2009 }}, accessed 2008-07-06</ref>

== Usage ==

=== Culinary use ===
[[File:Yakmomil-kkot-cha.jpg|thumb|Flowers picked for ''yakmomil-kkot-cha'' (flower tea) in ''[[sokuri]]'']]
It is commonly grown as a [[leaf vegetable]], and is used as a fresh herbal [[garnish (food)|garnish]].<ref name=pfaf/> The leaf has an unusual taste from its volatile oil {{ill|decanoyl acetaldehyde|qid=Q27149858}} (3-oxododecanal), a taste that is often described as "fishy", earning it the nickname "fish mint".

In northeastern India, the leaves are commonly used in salads, [[Salsa (Mexican cuisine)|salsas]], or cooked with other vegetables, and as a garnish over side dishes. The tender roots can also be ground into [[chutney]]s along with dry meat or fish, chilies, and [[tamarind]]. It is used raw as a salad and cooked along with fish as fish curry. In Japan and Korea, the dried leaves may be used as an [[Tisane|herbal tea]]. It is called ''dokudami-cha'' ({{lang|ja|どくだみ茶}}) in Japan and ''eoseongcho cha'' ({{lang|ko|어성초차}}) in Korea.

In Vietnamese cuisine, the plant is called ''diếp cá'' and is used with grilled meat and noodle salad dishes.<ref name="herbs">[https://vietherbs.com/herb-directory/fish-herb/ Vietnamese Herbs: Fish Mint], Accessed 9 October 2018.</ref> Fish mint may be used as a garnish with several Vietnamese dishes, such as ''[[gỏi cuốn]],'' stir-fried beef with fish mint salad, and ''[[bánh xèo]]''.<ref>[https://www.npr.org/2011/10/18/141470565/banh-xeo-sizzling-crepes, NPR Inc.:Banh Xeo (Sizzling Crepes)], Accessed 10 October 2018</ref>

[[File:Houttuynia_roots_vegetable_china.jpg|thumb|right|300px|Zhe'ergen is often served as a cold salad after being washed, chopped and tossed with sauces derived from vinegar, chili, coriander and soy sauce.]]
''Zhé'ěrgēn'' ([[Standard Chinese|Chinese]]: {{lang|zh|折耳根}}, "broken ear-root") is the edible rhizome of ''Houttuynia cordata'' (''yúxīngcǎo''; {{lang|zh|魚腥草}}; "fish-smelling grass") with a fresh, spicy, peppery flavour that is used in southwestern Chinese cuisine, i.e. that of [[Guizhou]], [[Sichuan]], [[Yunnan]] and western [[Guangxi]]. Typically the leaves are eaten in Sichuan and the root in Guizhou. ''Zhé'ěrgēn'' fried with larou (cured [[pork belly]]) is one of the staple dishes of Guizhou.
uses:
*part of the extensive [[fried rice]] cuisine of [[Guizhou]]
*a condiment to ''[[migan (noodle)|migan]]'' and ''[[mixian (noodle)|mixian]]'' noodles when served in broth
*as a component of dipping sauces used with the [[Shiping]] and [[Jianshui]] tradition of barbecued tofu
*raw consumption as part of cold-tossed salads, when it is most frequently combined with [[coriander]], [[vinegar]], fresh [[Chili pepper|chilli]], and [[soy sauce]].

=== Skincare ===
Extracts of this plant are a major ingredient in Korean skincare products.{{Citation needed|date=March 2025|reason=unreferenced fact}}
